records.quote: He loved baseball with a love passing the love of women, and the prospect of never seeing a game again in his life appalled him.
records.paraphrase: Birdsey is dismayed at the prospect of never seeing baseball again.

records.quote: He robbed the New Asiatic Bank of a hundred thousand dollars, jumped his bail, and was never heard of again.
records.paraphrase: Benyon's past crime and flight explain his years of hidden exile.

records.quote: It was because I was a dead man, and saw a chance of coming to life for a day; because I was sick of the damned tomb I've been living in for five centuries; because I've been aching for New York ever since I've left it
records.paraphrase: Benyon explains he risked capture out of longing for home after years of miserable exile.

records.quote: The man gave a start that was almost a leap, and the pallor of his face became a sickly white. His eyes, as he swung round, met Mr Birdsey's for an instant before they dropped, and there was panic fear in them.
records.paraphrase: The bearded man reacts with sudden panic and fear when tapped on the shoulder.

records.quote: If I think I remember a face, and can't place it, I worry myself into insomnia. It's partly sheer vanity, and partly because in my job a good memory for faces is a mighty fine asset.
records.paraphrase: Waterall describes his method of identifying faces from memory as central to his work.

records.quote: Even as the match gave out its flame, Mr Birdsey sprang.
records.paraphrase: Birdsey suddenly physically attacks Waterall to help Benyon escape.

records.quote: The next moment Benyon had broken down. His face was buried in his arms, and he was a wreck of a man, sobbing like a hurt child.
records.paraphrase: Benyon collapses emotionally after failing to use the pistol.

records.quote: He isn't a crook. He's a fan. And we exiled fans have got to stick together.
records.paraphrase: Birdsey contrasts the legal view of Benyon as a criminal with his own view of him as a fellow enthusiast.

records.quote: Mr Birdsey had been doing something which he had not done since he left New York five years ago. He had been watching a game of baseball.
records.paraphrase: The protagonist has been geographically separated from his home city for five years.

records.quote: This is Mr John Benyon, and I last saw him five years ago when I was a reporter in New York, and covered his trial.
records.paraphrase: The bearded stranger is revealed to be a fugitive whose identity Waterall recalls from a past trial.

criteria.rationale: The story is a contemporary comedic tale about baseball fans and a fugitive; no scientific facts, theories, discoveries, or speculative sciences are materially represented.
Only ordinary contemporary items appear (telephone, pistol, train, champagne). None is a speculative or engineered invention that materially shapes the setting or outcome; these are mundane tools.

The 'five centuries' phrase in ev07 is clearly a hyperbolic figure of speech for five years of exile (ev01), not actual temporal displacement, a speculative future, or remote past. The setting is contemporary.

The plot follows from an ordinary crime and personal circumstances (a bank robbery and social exile), not consequences extrapolated from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise in a speculative sense.
Waterall's recognition of a face by memory (ev04) is a personal knack and ordinary recall, not observation, hypothesis, testing, measurement, or systematic evidential inference driving understanding.
Locations are ordinary Earthly places (London, New York, Algiers). No other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them appear.
The only calamities are a personal bank robbery and individual misfortune (exile, potential arrest); there is no large-scale natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused disaster.

candidates.description: The situation of the 'exiled baseball fan' driven to extreme risk by longing for the game and home.

novelty.rationale: The 'exiled fan' is a sentimental and comic conceit, not a totalizing or world-altering difference from the empirical norm. Living abroad, missing baseball, and feeling homesick are entirely consistent with the ordinary contemporary world; nothing about the story universe is systematically altered.

cognitive_validation.rationale: With no novum to validate, there is no imaginary science or systematic social innovation to assess. The story operates entirely within mundane realist causation.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The theme of the exiled fan does govern the plot logic and the climactic decision to help Benyon escape, but centrality alone does not create a novum in the absence of novelty and cognitive innovation.

estrangement.rationale: The story generates mild reader-facing contrast between the legal framing of Benyon as a criminal and Birdsey's framing of him as a fellow fan, but this is a moral/sentimental contrast within a realist frame, not cognitive estrangement produced by a novum.

candidates.description: Waterall's cultivated memory-for-faces skill by which the fugitive is recognized.

novelty.rationale: An exceptional memory for faces is a mundane human talent, not a difference from the empirical norm. Nothing about the world is altered by it; it functions as an ordinary plot device.

cognitive_validation.rationale: There is no imaginary scientific or social system underlying the skill; it is described as vanity and professional habit, so there is nothing novum-like to validate.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The recognition triggers the plot but is an incidental realist device; it does not constitute an overriding world-defining logic.

estrangement.rationale: No cognitive estrangement arises; the recognition is an ordinary detective-fiction turn.
